pos: n. (a measure of distance; in the Authorized Version, the Roman mile Christ names in His teaching on nonresistance)
etymology: Latin mille passus, a thousand paces, the Roman soldier's measured stride multiplied a thousand times to mark distance along an imperial road. The word entered English carrying the very unit a Roman occupier would have used to measure forced labor.
biblical_def:
Christ's one use of the word sits inside the hardest paragraph of the Sermon on the Mount, the teaching on retaliation: after the cheek struck and turned again, after the coat surrendered along with the cloke, comes whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain. The word compel is doing real legal work here — it names the Roman right of impressment, by which any soldier could seize a subject of the empire and force him to carry a burden one mile, no more, under law. Simon of Cyrene, compelled to bear Christ's cross, is the same word in action a few chapters later.

Christ's command does not ask His hearers to resist the compulsion or even merely to comply with the letter of the law. It asks something the law did not require and the soldier had no right to demand: a second mile, freely walked, past the exact point where the legal claim on a man's labor ran out. The teaching does not abolish the injustice of the Roman mile-law; it answers it with a deliberate excess of willingness that the law itself could never have compelled, turning a forced labor into a voluntary gift the moment the first mile ends.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a measure of length or distance, in England and America equal to 1760 yards; among the Romans, a thousand paces.
webster_full: MILE, n. A measure of length or distance; the Roman mile was a thousand paces, about 1614 yards.
COMPEL, v.t. To force, to oblige, to constrain by physical, moral, or legal power.
TWAIN, a. Two; a pair; an old form still used in poetic or elevated speech.
CLOKE, n. A loose outer garment; figuratively, a pretext or covering for a real design.
RESIST, v.t. To withstand; to oppose; to strive against; to act in opposition to force or authority.
scriptures: Mat 5:40
And if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloke also.
Mat 5:41
And whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain.
Mat 5:42
Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away.
And as they came out, they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name: him they compelled to bear his cross.
corruption_summary: Christ's second-mile teaching is flattened into a general call to niceness, when it names a specific legal compulsion under Roman occupation and answers it with a deliberate excess the law could not demand.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself — a mile is still a mile. The principle worth recovering is the precise legal shape of the situation Christ describes. Impressment under Roman law had a fixed limit, one mile, and a Jewish subject under occupation had every worldly reason to walk exactly that far and not one step more, resenting every pace of it.

Christ's command works inside that limit rather than against it, converting the second mile from something the soldier could never lawfully demand into something the disciple freely gives. It is not passivity and it is not a general principle of unlimited compliance with every demand; it is a specific refusal to let a forced injustice set the boundary of a disciple's generosity, matching the cross Simon of Cyrene was compelled to carry with a willingness Christ Himself modeled all the way to Calvary.
roots_summary: Greek milion (G3400), a Roman mile, a loanword from Latin mille; aggareuo (G29), to press into service, the verb behind “compel” in both Matthew 5:41 and 27:32.
roots_lines: Greek milion (G3400) — a Roman mile, a thousand paces; a direct loanword from the Latin, used only at Matthew 5:41.
Greek aggareuo (G29) — to press into service, to compel by legal right of impressment; a Persian loanword for the courier system adopted by Rome.
Greek hupago (G5217) — to go, to go away, to depart; the plain verb of going the second mile.
Greek antistemi (G436) — to set against, to resist; the verb Christ forbids two verses earlier, Matthew 5:39.
Greek daneizo (G1155) — to lend; the verb of Matthew 5:42, closing the same paragraph on generosity beyond compulsion.
usage: “whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain” — Christ's teaching on the second mile.
“him they compelled to bear his cross” — the same compulsion falling on Simon of Cyrene.
“Give to him that asketh thee” — the generosity the second mile belongs to.

pos: n. (the natural fluid of a fruit or plant; sap; that which is pressed or expressed from a substance)
etymology: Old French jus, from Latin jus, broth or liquid. The word names the inward liquid of a living thing, what remains once the fruit itself has been pressed or crushed to yield it.
biblical_def:
The Song of Solomon's single use of the word belongs to its most intimate scene, the bride imagining her beloved welcomed into her mother's house: I would lead thee, and bring thee into my mother's house, who would instruct me: I would cause thee to drink of spiced wine of the juice of my pomegranate. The pomegranate, with its hundreds of seeds each cased in its own red, wine-dark juice, was already the Song's standing figure for the bride herself — her temples like a piece of pomegranate, her orchard an orchard of pomegranates with pleasant fruits. To offer the juice of her own pomegranate is to offer the fruit of a love the Song treats throughout as a garden shut up and a fountain sealed, opened now by invitation and not by force.

Nothing in the verse is vague or merely decorative. The spiced wine made from that juice is a prepared, cultivated gift, not a raw or careless one — the labor of tending an orchard stands behind every cup. Scripture's single use of juice therefore carries the whole Song's larger argument in miniature: that the deepest gifts of marriage are neither taken nor stolen but pressed out over time, offered freely, and received as exactly what they are, the fruit of patient cultivation rather than the plunder of appetite.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the sap or fluid part of vegetables and fruits, which may be expressed or extracted by pressure.
webster_full: JUICE, n. The sap of a plant or the fluid part of a fruit, expressed or extracted by pressure or otherwise.
POMEGRANATE, n. A fruit having a thick red rind and containing numerous seeds, each surrounded with a red, juicy pulp.
SPICED, a. Seasoned or flavored with aromatic substances; prepared with spice for pleasantness or preservation.
ORCHARD, n. A garden or enclosure devoted to the cultivation of fruit trees.
SEAL, v.t. To close up securely; to set a mark of ownership or authenticity upon; to make fast against opening.
scriptures: Son 8:2
I would lead thee, and bring thee into my mother's house, who would instruct me: I would cause thee to drink of spiced wine of the juice of my pomegranate.
Son 4:12
A garden inclosed is my sister, my spouse; a spring shut up, a fountain sealed.
Son 4:13
Thy plants are an orchard of pomegranates, with pleasant fruits; camphire, with spikenard,
Son 4:3
Thy lips are like a thread of scarlet, and thy speech is comely: thy temples are like a piece of a pomegranate within thy locks.
corruption_summary: The Song's garden imagery is either allegorized away from the body entirely or coarsened into mere appetite, when the juice of the pomegranate is offered in the text as a cultivated gift, pressed out over time and given freely, not seized.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; juice still names the pressed-out fluid of a fruit. The principle worth recovering runs against two opposite errors that have followed the Song of Solomon through much of its interpretive history. One spiritualizes every image so thoroughly that a real married love, with a real body and real fruit, disappears into pure allegory. The other reduces the same imagery to bare appetite, missing the patient cultivation the text insists on — a garden inclosed, a fountain sealed, an orchard tended before any fruit is offered.

The juice of the pomegranate in chapter eight is offered, not taken, by a bride who has spent the whole Song describing an orchard grown and guarded rather than a fruit simply plucked. Marriage as Scripture pictures it here is neither prudish silence about the body nor appetite loosed from all cultivation, but a gift pressed out in its own season and given by the one whose garden it is.
roots_summary: Hebrew asiys (H6071), sweet or fresh wine, pressed juice; the noun behind the “juice” of the pomegranate in Song of Solomon 8:2.
roots_lines: Hebrew asiys (H6071) — sweet wine, fresh-pressed juice; the noun rendered “juice” in Song of Solomon 8:2.
Hebrew rimmon (H7416) — a pomegranate; the fruit named repeatedly through the Song as a figure of the bride.
Hebrew gan na'ul — a garden shut up, a garden inclosed; the standing figure of Song of Solomon 4:12 for guarded love.
Hebrew ma'yan chathum — a sealed fountain; paired with the enclosed garden in the same verse.
Hebrew pardec (H6508) — an orchard, a park, a paradise-garden; a Persian loanword naming the cultivated orchard of Song 4:13.
usage: “I would cause thee to drink of spiced wine of the juice of my pomegranate” — the bride's offered gift.
“A garden inclosed is my sister, my spouse; a spring shut up, a fountain sealed” — the guarded love that gift completes.
“Thy plants are an orchard of pomegranates, with pleasant fruits” — the cultivation standing behind the offered juice.

pos: n. (a pungent bulbous vegetable of the lily family; in the Authorized Version, part of the remembered fare of Egypt)
etymology: Old French oignon, from Latin unio, oneness, unity — the Romans named the vegetable for its single, undivided bulb, in contrast to garlic's many separate cloves. A humble vegetable carrying, by pure etymological accident, the word for oneness at its root.
biblical_def:
Numbers records the onion among the small catalogue of Egyptian food the wilderness generation suddenly remembers with longing: We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick. Every item on the list is ordinary and cheap, the ration of slaves rather than the delicacy of kings, and that is precisely the force of the complaint. Israel is not longing for Egyptian luxury; she is longing for Egyptian bondage, remembered now as freedom because it came with flavor, while the manna God provides fresh each morning is despised as tasteless.

The chapter's severity toward this complaint — a plague breaking out even while the meat is still between their teeth — is out of all proportion to onions and garlick considered merely as food, and that disproportion is the point. What Israel actually craved, wrapped inside a grocery list, was the whole condition of Egypt itself, remembered selectively and falsely as a table of freely available food rather than what it actually was, the house of bondage the LORD had just brought them out of at tremendous cost. The onion, the least of the items named, exposes how thoroughly memory can be seasoned to taste by an ungrateful heart.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a well known bulbous plant of the genus Allium, cultivated for its pungent, edible root.
webster_full: ONION, n. A plant and its bulbous root, of a strong, pungent smell and taste, much used for food and seasoning.
LEEK, n. A plant of the onion family, with a milder flavor, cultivated as a pot-herb.
MANNA, n. The food miraculously supplied to the Israelites in the wilderness; figuratively, spiritual nourishment from God.
LUST, v.i. To have vehement desire; to long for with intensity, often of an unlawful or excessive appetite.
BONDAGE, n. Slavery; the state of being bound to service; a state of involuntary servitude.
scriptures: Num 11:5
We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick:
Num 11:6
But now our soul is dried away: there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes.

But even a whole month, until it come out at your nostrils, and it be loathsome unto you: because that ye have despised the LORD which is among you, and have wept before him, saying, Why came we forth out of Egypt?
Exo 16:3

And the children of Israel said unto them, Would to God we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the flesh pots, and when we did eat bread to the full; for ye have brought us forth into this wilderness, to kill this whole assembly with hunger.
corruption_summary: Nostalgia for a former bondage is dressed up as a legitimate grievance about present hardship, when Numbers exposes the onions and leeks of Egypt as a taste-memory that has quietly rewritten slavery as freedom.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain vegetable. The principle worth recovering is how the text treats the complaint built around it. Israel's list of remembered food is accurate as far as it goes — Egypt did have fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlick — and the complaint's plausibility is exactly what makes it dangerous, because it lets a real and terrible bondage be remembered as a table freely spread.

The LORD's response, giving them meat until it comes out at their nostrils and becomes loathsome, is aimed not at the food itself but at the despising underneath it — a rejection of present provision rooted in a falsified memory of the past. The onion is the least item on the list and, for that very reason, the clearest evidence of how completely craving had replaced gratitude: it is not a great injustice being protested here, only garlick, and the whole camp is willing to call God's daily bread worthless next to it.
roots_summary: Hebrew betsel (H1211), an onion; part of a short catalogue of Egyptian vegetables named only here in the whole Old Testament.
roots_lines: Hebrew betsel (H1211) — an onion; found only in Numbers 11:5 in the entire Hebrew Bible.
Hebrew chatsiyr (H2682) — leek, grass, herb; the word just before it in the same list.
Hebrew shum (H7762) — garlick; closing the short list of remembered Egyptian food.
Hebrew man (H4478) — manna; the daily bread despised in the same breath the onions are craved.
Hebrew ta'ab (H8354/H183, from avah) — to lust, to crave intensely; the verb naming Israel's condition in Numbers 11:4.
usage: “the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlick” — the remembered fare of Egypt.
“there is nothing at all, beside this manna, before our eyes” — the daily provision despised alongside it.
“because that ye have despised the LORD which is among you” — the real charge underneath the craving.

pos: n. (a narrow way beaten by the feet of travelers; a track or footpath)
etymology: A compound of path, Saxon paeth, a trodden track, and way, the ground traveled over. A pathway is smaller and more particular than a way — the actual worn line of feet across a field, not the road itself.
biblical_def:
Proverbs' single use of the word closes a proverb built on a stark either-or: In the way of righteousness is life; and in the pathway thereof there is no death. The structure repeats the same claim twice with two different words for the same trodden ground — the way of righteousness, and then its pathway, its own particular worn track — as if to insist that life is not merely the destination of righteousness but its whole visible course, every footstep of it, not death waiting somewhere further down the same road.

The proverb belongs to a chapter thick with the same contrast, the way of the wicked seduced and the way of the just made plain, and it reads more sharply for how absolute its second half is. Not fewer deaths along the pathway of righteousness, not death delayed, but no death in it at all, the same confidence Christ later grounds in Himself when He calls His own person the way, the truth, and the life. A pathway, by its nature, is a track other feet have already worn; Proverbs' claim is that the specific pathway of righteousness has been worn by feet that did not, in the end, walk it into death.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a narrow way or path; a track beaten by the feet of men or animals, distinct from a road for carriages.
webster_full: PATHWAY, n. A narrow foot-path; a way beaten by the feet of passengers, as distinguished from a road.
WAY, n. A road, path, or track; also, a course of conduct or manner of life.
RIGHTEOUSNESS, n. Purity of heart and rectitude of life; conformity of life to the divine law.
SEDUCE, v.t. To lead astray; to entice from the path of duty or rectitude by deceit or flattery.
PLAIN, a. Open; clear; evident; free from obstruction or ambiguity; easily understood.
scriptures: In the way of righteousness is life; and in the pathway thereof there is no death.
The righteous is more excellent than his neighbour: but the way of the wicked seduceth them.
The way of life is above to the wise, that he may depart from hell beneath.
Joh 14:6
Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
corruption_summary: Righteousness is treated as a destination reached at the end of a life, while the road itself is assumed to run through the same losses and death as any other path, when Proverbs insists the pathway itself, not merely its end, carries no death in it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; a pathway is still a worn track underfoot. The principle worth recovering is the sharpness of the proverb's grammar — it does not say the way of righteousness leads eventually to life while passing through death along the way, but that the pathway itself, its whole visible course, has no death in it.

Proverbs fifteen supplies the picture beneath the claim, a way of life running above so that a man departs from hell beneath, and John's Gospel supplies its final ground: Christ does not point to a way, He is the way, and the truth, and the life. The pathway of righteousness has no death in it because the one who walks ahead of every believer on it has already walked through death and out the other side; the track is worn by feet a believer is simply following.
roots_summary: Hebrew nathiyb (H5410), a beaten path, a well-worn way; paired with derek (H1870), the broader way, in the parallel structure of Proverbs 12:28.
roots_lines: Hebrew nathiyb (H5410) — a path, a beaten track; the word rendered “pathway” in Proverbs 12:28, the narrower of the two parallel terms.
Hebrew derek (H1870) — a way, a road, a course of life; the broader word paired with it in the same verse.
Hebrew tsedaqah (H6666) — righteousness; the quality whose way and pathway the proverb describes.
Hebrew mavet (H4194) — death; explicitly and absolutely excluded from the pathway of righteousness.
Greek hodos (G3598) — a way, a road, a journey; the very word Christ applies to Himself in John 14:6.
usage: “In the way of righteousness is life; and in the pathway thereof there is no death” — the whole proverb.
“The way of life is above to the wise, that he may depart from hell beneath” — the same contrast from Proverbs fifteen.
“I am the way, the truth, and the life” — the pathway's own claim about itself, in Christ's mouth.

pos: n. (the removal or lightening of distress, want, or pain; assistance sent to the needy)
etymology: Old French relief, from relever, to raise up again, itself from Latin re- and levare, to lift. Relief is, at root, a lifting back up — the reversal of a weight that had pressed a person down.
biblical_def:
Acts records the church at Antioch's first recorded act of organized giving in response to a specific, named need: Agabus prophesies a coming dearth, and immediately, without waiting for the famine to arrive, the disciples, every man according to his ability, determined to send relief unto the brethren which dwelt in Judaea. The relief is sent before the crisis fully lands, proportioned to what each man actually had rather than to some flat, equal share, and carried by named men, Barnabas and Saul, entrusted with the elders' own hands to see it delivered.

What the verse quietly establishes is a pattern the rest of the New Testament will return to often: the church's care for its own poor is not incidental charity but an expected, organized response to real news of real want, crossing real distance — a Gentile-heavy church at Antioch sending relief to Jewish believers in far-off Judaea, bound to them not by nationality but by the same body of Christ. Relief, in this one small notice, is shown doing exactly what its root name promises: lifting back up a body of believers about to be pressed down by a famine they had not yet even felt.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the removal, in whole or in part, of any evil, as pain, distress, or want; help; succor administered.
webster_full: RELIEF, n. The removal or alleviation of pain, grief, or distress; help afforded in time of need.
DEARTH, n. Scarcity, especially of food; a want or lack producing distress.
ABILITY, n. Power or capacity to do a thing; the means or resources by which something is accomplished.
DETERMINE, v.t. To resolve; to decide; to fix the course or purpose of the mind conclusively.
ELDER, n. A person who, by office or age, has oversight and authority in a church or community.
scriptures: And in these days came prophets from Jerusalem unto Antioch.
And there stood up one of them named Agabus, and signified by the spirit that there should be great dearth throughout all the world: which came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar.
Then the disciples, every man according to his ability, determined to send relief unto the brethren which dwelt in Judaea:
Which also they did, and sent it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul.
corruption_summary: Relief is treated as a purely secular welfare function, disconnected from the church, when Acts records it as the earliest organized act of a Gentile-heavy congregation, sent to distant Jewish believers precisely because both were one body.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; relief still names help sent to lighten distress. The principle worth recovering is how ordinary and unceremonious Acts makes the whole transaction. No debate over whether Antioch owed Judaea anything is recorded; a prophecy of dearth is given, and relief is simply determined on, each man giving according to his ability, before the famine has even struck.

The relief crosses a real social boundary the early church might easily have let stand — a largely Gentile church, only recently even permitted to receive the gospel without circumcision, sending material aid to Jewish believers in Judaea. That the gift is entrusted to Barnabas and Saul, carried by name and by hand to the elders, shows relief functioning here exactly as the New Testament elsewhere insists it must: not a vague sentiment but a specific, accountable, delivered act of the whole body caring for one part of itself.
roots_summary: Greek diakonia (G1248), service, ministry, the word behind organized relief throughout Acts; euporeo (G2141), to have ability, to prosper, behind “according to his ability.”
roots_lines: Greek diakonia (G1248) — service, ministry, the act of relief; the standing New Testament word for organized material aid to the needy.
Greek euporeo (G2141) — to have means, to prosper, to be well supplied; the verb behind “according to his ability” in Acts 11:29.
Greek limos (G3042) — famine, dearth, hunger; Agabus's own prophesied word.
Greek presbuteros (G4245) — elder; the office to whom the relief was formally delivered.
Greek koinonia (G2842) — fellowship, partnership, contribution; the broader New Testament word for the shared-giving Antioch's relief exemplifies.
usage: “there should be great dearth throughout all the world” — Agabus's prophecy that prompted the relief.
“every man according to his ability, determined to send relief” — the proportioned, voluntary giving of Antioch.
“sent it to the elders by the hands of Barnabas and Saul” — the accountable delivery of that relief.

pos: v.t. (to be like or similar to; to bear a likeness to in form, quality, or manner)
etymology: Old French resembler, from Latin re-, again, and similare, to be similar, from similis, like. To resemble is to be found again in another form — the same essential pattern showing up a second time in a different subject.
biblical_def:
The word's two Old and New Testament uses sit at very different heights. Gideon, questioning the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna about the men they had killed at Tabor, is answered with a single devastating detail: each one resembled the children of a king. The resemblance is enough for Gideon to know, before the kings finish speaking, exactly who those slain men were — his own brothers — and the whole scene turns on how much a physical likeness alone can disclose, and how much blood-debt that disclosure sets in motion.

Christ's use of the word, in the parable of the mustard seed, works at the opposite scale, likeness stretched to cover the whole shape of the kingdom of God: Unto what is the kingdom of God like? and whereunto shall I resemble it? The answer, a grain of mustard seed grown into a tree sheltering birds in its branches, resembles the kingdom not by being identical to it but by sharing its essential pattern — small, hidden, and destined for a growth out of all proportion to its beginning. Between Gideon's brothers, resembled and thereby recognized, and the kingdom, resembled and thereby explained, Scripture uses the word for exactly the work resemblance is suited to: disclosing a hidden identity through a visible likeness, without claiming the likeness and the thing itself are one and the same.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to be like; to have a similitude to, in appearance, qualities, or nature; to compare, as one thing to another.
webster_full: RESEMBLE, v.t. To be like; to have similitude to; also, to compare one thing with another for the sake of illustration.
LIKENESS, n. Resemblance; similitude; a form or figure representing another.
PARABLE, n. A fictitious narrative or comparison used to illustrate some moral or spiritual truth.
MUSTARD, n. A plant with a small seed, proverbial in the East for growing into a shrub of great size.
SLAY, v.t. To kill; to put to death, especially by violence.
scriptures: Jdg 8:18
Then said he unto Zebah and Zalmunna, What manner of men were they whom ye slew at Tabor? And they answered, As thou art, so were they; each one resembled the children of a king.
Jdg 8:19
And he said, They were my brethren, even the sons of my mother: as the LORD liveth, if ye had saved them alive, I would not slay you.
Then said he, Unto what is the kingdom of God like? and whereunto shall I resemble it?
It is like a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and cast into his garden; and it grew, and waxed a great tree; and the fowls of the air lodged in the branches of it.
corruption_summary: Resemblance is treated as a shallow surface similarity, a mere matter of appearance, when Scripture uses it in both its scenes to disclose a true and weighty identity that a casual glance would have missed entirely.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word. The principle worth recovering is how much theological and narrative weight Scripture is willing to place on a resemblance. Gideon's whole act of vengeance in the rest of the chapter turns on four words from a captured king — each one resembled the children of a king — a bare physical likeness carrying the full force of a recognized kinship and a demanded reckoning.

Christ's parable trusts resemblance with an even larger task: explaining the kingdom of God, an entirely spiritual and largely invisible reality, by comparison to a visible, ordinary seed. In neither case does Scripture confuse the resemblance with the thing itself — the slain men were not literally royal sons, and the kingdom is not literally a shrub — but in both cases the resemblance is treated as genuinely disclosive, a true likeness able to reveal what a direct look could not yet see.
roots_summary: Hebrew toar (H8389), form, appearance, figure; the noun behind “resembled” in Judges 8:18; Greek homoioo (G3666), to make like, behind Christ's parabolic use.
roots_lines: Hebrew toar (H8389) — form, figure, appearance; the noun underlying “resembled the children of a king” in Judges 8:18.
Hebrew melek (H4428) — a king; the standard the slain men's appearance was measured against.
Greek homoioo (G3666) — to make like, to liken, to compare; Christ's own verb in Luke 13:18, the root of the word parable in its comparative sense.
Greek kokkos sinapeos (G2848/G4615) — a grain of mustard seed; the small beginning Christ compares to the kingdom.
Greek klados (G2798) — a branch; where the fowls of the air lodge once the small seed becomes a great tree.
usage: “each one resembled the children of a king” — the resemblance that named Gideon's slain brothers.
“Unto what is the kingdom of God like? and whereunto shall I resemble it?” — Christ's own parabolic question.
“It is like a grain of mustard seed” — the resemblance Christ chooses to answer it.

pos: n. (the skin covering the top of the head, on which the hair grows)
etymology: Of uncertain origin, possibly related to Old Norse skalpr, a sheath or shell — the head's own natural covering, the surface a man's hair grows from and, in the Psalm's one use, the surface that most visibly betrays a habit of unrepented sin.
biblical_def:
The sixty-eighth Psalm, a triumphant march through the LORD's victories from Sinai to Zion, ends its catalogue of enemies with a single unsettling image: God shall wound the head of his enemies, and the hairy scalp of such an one as goeth on still in his trespasses. The wound is not aimed at just any enemy but specifically at one who goeth on still — not a man who has sinned once and repented, but one who persists, continues, keeps walking the same trespass without turning from it, verse after verse of the same unbroken habit.

The scalp, hairy and exposed, is the most visible and most personally identifying part of a man — the part by which he is known at a glance, uncovered, unable to be disguised by armor or clothing. That the wound falls there rather than elsewhere in the body is the Psalm's own quiet argument: persistent, unrepented trespass is not hidden from God the way a man might hope to hide it from his neighbors, and the judgment that finally falls on it falls precisely on the part of him that has always been in plain view. The Psalm's larger movement, from Sinai's fire to Zion's sanctuary, frames this one grim image with an entire chapter of the LORD's care for the fatherless, the widow, and the prisoner — the same God who wounds the persistent trespasser is, in the same Psalm, the one who sets the solitary in families.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the skin which covers the top of the head; also, among some nations, this skin torn off as a trophy of war.
webster_full: SCALP, n. The skin of the head, on which the hair grows; the integument covering the skull.
WOUND, v.t. To hurt or injure by violence; to pierce or cut so as to cause harm.
TRESPASS, n. An offense; a sin; a violation of duty or of another's rights, especially a continuing or habitual one.
PERSIST, v.i. To continue steadily in a purpose or course, especially against opposition or obstacles.
SANCTUARY, n. A sacred place; a place set apart for the worship of God; hence, a place of refuge or protection.
scriptures: He that is our God is the God of salvation; and unto GOD the Lord belong the issues from death.
But God shall wound the head of his enemies, and the hairy scalp of such an one as goeth on still in his trespasses.
Psa 68:5
A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows, is God in his holy habitation.
Psa 68:6
God setteth the solitary in families: he bringeth out those which are bound with chains: but the rebellious dwell in a dry land.
corruption_summary: Persistent, unrepented sin is treated as invisible, a private matter no one else can see, when the Psalm locates its judgment precisely on the part of a man that has always been in plain view, the hairy scalp no covering can hide.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; a scalp is still the skin of the head. The principle worth recovering is the Psalm's careful qualifier — the wound does not fall on every enemy or every sinner, but specifically on one who goeth on still in his trespasses, a present, continuous, unbroken habit rather than a single fall.

Read beside the Psalm's own portrait of God as a father of the fatherless and a judge of widows, the image is not a picture of divine cruelty but of exact justice matched to exact persistence — the same God who sets the solitary in families and brings prisoners into prosperity is the one who will not let a habitual, ongoing trespass hide behind the appearance of an ordinary head of hair. What is most visible about a man, in the end, is not hidden from the God whose Psalm this is.
roots_summary: Hebrew qodqod (H6936), the crown of the head, the scalp; the same word used at Genesis 49:26 of Joseph's own crowned head, here turned to judgment.
roots_lines: Hebrew qodqod (H6936) — the crown or top of the head, the scalp; used both of blessing (Genesis 49:26, Deuteronomy 33:16) and, here, of judgment.
Hebrew se'ar (H8181) — hair; the adjective “hairy” built on this root, describing the exposed, unmistakable scalp.
Hebrew halak (H1980, in the reflexive stem) — to go on, to walk continually; the verb behind “goeth on still,” naming ongoing habit rather than a single fall.
Hebrew asham (H817, related to trespass offerings) — guilt, trespass; the state named by the one persisting.
Hebrew machats (H4272) — to smite, to wound, to shatter; the verb of God's own action against the persistent enemy.
usage: “God shall wound the head of his enemies, and the hairy scalp” — the Psalm's judgment on habitual trespass.
“such an one as goeth on still in his trespasses” — the qualifier that narrows the judgment's target.
“A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows” — the same God's care, framing the same Psalm.

pos: n. (the blade of a plow that cuts the ground; also, a portion allotted or divided among several)
etymology: Saxon scearu, from sceran, to shear or cut — the same root as shear and shard. A plowshare is, at root, simply the cutting blade, the part of the plow that shears the ground open.
biblical_def:
First Samuel's one use of the word belongs to a scene of deliberate, systematic disarmament: the Philistines, having conquered Israel's smiths, force every Israelite to sharpen every man his share, and his coulter, and his axe, and his mattock down at the Philistine forge, at a fixed and extortionate price, so that no Israelite blacksmith remains who could also forge a sword or a spear. The share named here is agricultural, not military — the plowshare's blade, meant to cut furrows, not men — and its careful listing alongside the coulter, axe, and mattock underlines exactly how thorough the disarmament was: even ordinary farm tools had to be maintained at the enemy's mercy.

The verse is worth reading against the prophetic image the Old Testament repeats twice, in Isaiah and Micah, of nations who shall beat their swords into plowshares in the age when the LORD judges between many peoples and war is learned no more. First Samuel shows the image running in the opposite, grimmer direction: a people with no swords left to beat into plowshares because their plowshares themselves have been placed under an enemy's thumb. Between the two texts stands the whole distance between a peace imposed by conquest, which strips even a farmer's tools of independence, and the peace promised by the LORD, in which the very metal of war is willingly, not forcibly, turned to feed a people rather than to fight them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the iron blade of a plow, which cuts the ground and prepares it for the furrow.
webster_full: SHARE, n. The part of a plow which cuts or opens the ground, usually of iron or steel.
COULTER, n. The sharp iron blade of a plow fixed before the share, cutting the earth in a vertical line.
MATTOCK, n. A tool resembling a pickaxe, used for grubbing up roots or digging hard ground.
SMITH, n. One who works in metals, especially iron; a forger of tools or weapons.
PLOWSHARE, n. The share or blade of a plow; used figuratively of instruments of peaceful labor as opposed to war.
scriptures: Now there was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel: for the Philistines said, Lest the Hebrews make them swords or spears:
But all the Israelites went down to the Philistines, to sharpen every man his share, and his coulter, and his axe, and his mattock.
Isa 2:4

And he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people: and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.
Mic 4:3

And he shall judge among many people, and rebuke strong nations afar off; and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up a sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.
corruption_summary: The prophetic image of swords beaten into plowshares is invoked as a general slogan for peace, when the plowshares of 1 Samuel show the same tool under a very different, coerced peace imposed by conquest rather than chosen by covenant.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain tool. The principle worth recovering is the sharp contrast between the two biblical scenes that mention plowshares. In 1 Samuel, Israel's plowshares are not beaten from swords by a free people choosing peace; they are the last tools a conquered people is permitted to keep, and even those must be sharpened under the conqueror's price and control.

The prophetic vision of Isaiah and Micah describes something categorically different: a peace that follows the LORD's own judgment among the nations, chosen and permanent, in which swords become plowshares because war itself has been judged and ended, not because a conquering power has simply confiscated the swords. Reading 1 Samuel's share beside the prophets' plowshare shows that peace imposed by force and peace given by the LORD's own reign may share a tool's name and still be worlds apart in substance.
roots_summary: Hebrew machareshah (H4282), a plowshare, a mattock; the word behind “share” in 1 Samuel 13:20, distinct from the plowshares of the prophetic vision.
roots_lines: Hebrew machareshah (H4282) — a plowshare or mattock; the noun rendered “share” in 1 Samuel 13:20.
Hebrew eth (H855) — a plowshare, a coulter; the parallel term paired with it in the same verse.
Hebrew chereb (H2719) — a sword; the weapon expressly denied to Israel by the Philistines' policy.
Hebrew ittiym (H855, plural of eth) — plowshares; the same root Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3 use of swords beaten into peace.
Hebrew mazmerah (H4211) — a pruninghook; paired with plowshares in both prophetic visions of universal peace.
usage: “to sharpen every man his share, and his coulter, and his axe, and his mattock” — Israel's tools under Philistine control.
“there was no smith found throughout all the land of Israel” — the disarmament behind that dependence.
“they shall beat their swords into plowshares” — the very different peace the prophets promise.

pos: n. (shelter from heat or light; comparative darkness caused by interception of the sun's rays)
etymology: Saxon sceadu, shadow, shade — the same root as shadow, from which shade is not sharply distinguished in older English. What casts a shade stands between a person and a heat that would otherwise fall directly upon him.
biblical_def:
The Song of Ascents that is Psalm 121 spends its whole short length answering one question, where help comes from, and its middle verses give the answer its most physically vivid form: The LORD is thy keeper: the LORD is thy shade upon thy right hand. The image is of a pilgrim on the road up to Jerusalem, sun beating down through the heat of the day, and instead of a tree or a rock offering relief, it is the LORD Himself, positioned at the traveler's right hand, functioning as his personal shade against the very thing that would otherwise wear him down mile by mile.

The verses immediately following make the promise even more comprehensive: The sun shall not smite thee by day, nor the moon by night — shade against the sun's heat and, in the ancient world's own reckoning, protection from whatever harm the night and its moon were feared to bring as well. The Psalm never claims the pilgrim's road will be shortened or the heat removed from the world; it claims the LORD Himself will stand where the shade is needed, at exactly the hand where a traveler would naturally look for support. A psalm meant to be sung on pilgrimage gives its plainest comfort in the plainest possible image: not that the journey will be easy, but that the shade will not fail along the way.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a place sheltered from the sun's rays; comparative obscurity or darkness caused by the interception of light.
webster_full: SHADE, n. Comparative darkness caused by the interruption of the rays of light; a shelter from heat or glare.
KEEPER, n. One who guards, watches, or has the care and custody of a person or thing.
SMITE, v.t. To strike; to afflict, injure, or destroy, especially by a sudden or heavy blow.
PILGRIM, n. A wanderer or traveler, especially one journeying to a sacred place for religious purposes.
ASCENT, n. The act of rising or climbing; a way or path leading upward, as to a height or a holy place.
scriptures: The LORD is thy keeper: the LORD is thy shade upon thy right hand.
The sun shall not smite thee by day, nor the moon by night.
A Song of degrees. I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help.
The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore.
corruption_summary: Shade is treated as passive relief from a difficulty already removed, when the Psalm names it as active, personal protection given precisely while the sun still beats and the journey still continues.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; shade still names shelter from heat or light. The principle worth recovering is what the Psalm does and does not promise. It does not say the sun's heat will be turned off or the road up to Jerusalem shortened; it says the LORD Himself will be positioned exactly where a traveler needs relief, at his right hand, for as long as the climb continues.

The Psalm's closing promise, that the LORD shall preserve a man's going out and coming in from this time forth and even for evermore, reveals that the shade of verse five is not a single moment's comfort but a standing arrangement for the whole of the pilgrimage, this journey and every one after it. A shade that only appeared once the heat had already passed would be no comfort at all; the Psalm's confidence rests on a shade given precisely at the hour of the sun's full strength.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsel (H6738), shade, shadow, protection; the word applied to the LORD Himself in Psalm 121:5, and elsewhere to the shadow of His wings.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsel (H6738) — shade, shadow; the noun applied directly to the LORD as protector in Psalm 121:5.
Hebrew shamar (H8104) — to keep, to guard, to watch over; the verb behind “keeper,” repeated six times through this short Psalm.
Hebrew yamiyn (H3225) — the right hand; the position of honor and support where the LORD is said to stand.
Hebrew nakah (H5221) — to smite, to strike; the harm the sun and moon are here forbidden to inflict.
Hebrew ma'aleh (H4609, from the title Song of Degrees/Ascents) — a going up, an ascent; the pilgrimage setting of the whole Psalm.
usage: “The LORD is thy keeper: the LORD is thy shade upon thy right hand” — the Psalm's central image.
“The sun shall not smite thee by day, nor the moon by night” — the shade's full, round-the-clock scope.
“The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in” — the same shade extended over the whole of life.

pos: n. (a gate, especially of a city or fortress; in the Authorized Version, one of the gates of rebuilt Jerusalem)
etymology: Latin porta, a gate or entrance, from portare, to carry — the passage through which what is carried in and out of a city must go. The same root gives portal and portico.
biblical_def:
Nehemiah's night ride around the ruined walls of Jerusalem, before he has told anyone what God has put in his heart to do, passes a gate the Authorized Version names with this older word for a city entrance: I went out by night by the gate of the valley, even before the dragon well, and to the dung port, and viewed the walls of Jerusalem, which were broken down, and the gates thereof were consumed with fire. The dung port, or dung gate, was the passage by which the city's refuse was carried out — the least honored of Jerusalem's gates by function, and yet the first one Nehemiah's own survey specifically names, riding past it in the dark to assess exactly how much rebuilding a broken wall would require.

What makes the detail worth keeping is the pattern the rest of the book confirms: this same unglamorous dung gate is later rebuilt, named by name, in the third chapter's careful list of every section of wall and every family that repaired it, with no less care given to its repair than to any other gate in the city. Nehemiah's survey does not skip the least honorable entrance to save time, and the builders do not leave it broken because no one would notice. A city's walls, in this book, are only as whole as their least regarded port, and the rebuilding accounts for every one of them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a gate, especially of a city, castle, or fortified place; an entrance or passage.
webster_full: PORT, n. A gate; an entrance, especially of a fortified town or city; also, a harbor for ships.
WALL, n. A structure of stone, brick, or other material, raised to enclose or defend a place.
VIEW, v.t. To see; to survey; to examine with the eye, especially with care or deliberation.
DUNG, n. Excrement; refuse matter, especially that used or removed as waste.
REPAIR, v.t. To restore to a sound or good state after decay, injury, or dilapidation.
scriptures: Neh 2:12
And I arose in the night, I and some few men with me; neither told I any man what my God had put in my heart to do at Jerusalem: neither was there any beast with me, save the beast that I rode upon.
Neh 2:13

And I went out by night by the gate of the valley, even before the dragon well, and to the dung port, and viewed the walls of Jerusalem, which were broken down, and the gates thereof were consumed with fire.
Neh 3:13

The valley gate repaired Hanun, and the inhabitants of Zanoah; they built it, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof, and a thousand cubits on the wall unto the dung gate.
Neh 3:14
But the dung gate repaired Malchiah the son of Rechab, the ruler of part of Bethhaccerem; he built it, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof.
corruption_summary: The least visible or least honored parts of a shared work are treated as safe to leave undone, when Nehemiah's own night survey and the builders' own roster give the dung port the same careful attention given to every other gate of the city.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; a port here is simply a gate. The principle worth recovering is Nehemiah's own thoroughness before a single stone is laid. Riding alone at night, unannounced, he surveys the dung port along with the gate of the valley and every other breach, refusing to let the least honorable gate go unassessed merely because it carried the city's refuse rather than its dignitaries.

The third chapter's building roster completes the point: Malchiah the son of Rechab, ruler of part of Bethhaccerem, is named by name as the man who repaired the dung gate, its doors, its locks, and its bars, with exactly the same formula given to every more prominent gate in the same chapter. Nehemiah's Jerusalem is rebuilt whole, not selectively, and its least regarded port is written into the record with the same specific, personal credit given to its most honored one.
roots_summary: Hebrew sha'ar (H8179), a gate, a port; the ordinary word for the whole series of city gates named through Nehemiah two and three.
roots_lines: Hebrew sha'ar (H8179) — a gate, a port, an entrance; the standard word for every gate named in Nehemiah's survey and rebuilding.
Hebrew ashpoth (H830) — dung, refuse; the word giving the dung gate its name.
Hebrew chazaq (H2388, in the sense of repair) — to strengthen, to repair; the verb repeated through Nehemiah 3 of every builder's own section of wall.
Hebrew chomah (H2346) — a wall, a fortification; the structure whose breaches Nehemiah surveys by night.
Hebrew tanniyn (H8577, root of “dragon”) — a dragon, a sea-monster; the well named beside the dung port in Nehemiah 2:13, of uncertain identification.
usage: “I went out by night... and to the dung port, and viewed the walls of Jerusalem” — Nehemiah's private survey.
“the dung gate repaired Malchiah the son of Rechab” — the same gate's careful, credited repair.
“neither told I any man what my God had put in my heart” — the quiet diligence behind the whole survey.
